title: Assessing Fitness to Travel: Practical Cases in Air Travel and Chronic Disease Management
description: Case-based quiz (Q1–Q10) covering COPD and hypoxia testing, post-MI/PCI air travel, and the multi-morbid traveller. Source: lecture slides, 2026-10-16.

questions.text: Based on the information provided, which is the most appropriate next step in assessing this patient's fitness to fly?
options: He is fit to fly without further assessment because his resting SpO₂ is >90%.
Prescribe in-flight oxygen immediately because his FEV₁ is <40% predicted.
Perform a detailed pre-flight assessment, including resting oxygen saturation and functional capacity, and consider formal hypoxia testing.
Perform spirometry again immediately; the decision should be based primarily on the current FEV₁.

questions.text: Which feature in this patient most strongly supports proceeding to formal hypoxia testing before a long-haul flight?
options: Age of 68 years alone
Former smoking history
FEV₁ of 38% predicted with resting SpO₂ of 93% on room air
Not currently using home oxygen

questions.text: His hypoxic challenge test produces a PaO₂ of 7.0 kPa (53 mmHg) with SpO₂ of 82%, and he remains clinically stable. Which is the most appropriate management?
options: No special arrangement is needed because his PaO₂ remains >50 mmHg.
Recommend supplemental oxygen during the flight and arrange the airline's oxygen requirements in advance.
Cancel all air travel permanently because the HCT is abnormal.
Start long-term home oxygen before the trip as soon as possible.

questions.text: A 55-year-old has an uncomplicated STEMI treated with successful primary PCI, preserved EF, no arrhythmia. He wants the earliest reasonable date to take a 2-hour flight. What do you advise?
options: He should never fly again
From about 3 days (many clinicians advise 7–10 days)
Only after 3 months
Only after a normal exercise stress test, mandatory

questions.text: Which of the following is the most important consideration when deciding whether she can fly on day 9 after her NSTEMI?
options: The fact that she is receiving dual antiplatelet therapy
Whether the myocardial infarction and PCI have been clinically uncomplicated and she is stable
Whether her EF has returned to ≥55%
Whether she has been discharged from hospital for at least 7 days

questions.text: What additional concern is particularly relevant because this is a 13-hour long-haul flight?
options: Increased risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and the challenges of prolonged immobility
Increased risk of acute stent thrombosis caused directly by cabin pressure
A predictable reduction in EF caused by the lower cabin oxygen concentration
Loss of antiplatelet effect caused by prolonged exposure to cabin altitude

questions.text: Before completing the airline's MEDIF, which finding would most strongly support advising her to postpone the flight?
options: She remains clinically stable, has no chest pain or heart failure, and can walk without significant symptoms
She is taking DAPT following implantation of a drug-eluting stent
She has persistent/recurrent chest pain, decompensated heart failure, or another sign of ongoing cardiac instability
Her EF is 45% with no symptoms or clinical evidence of heart failure

questions.text: Which of the following best summarizes the key issues that should be addressed before clearing this patient for the flight?
options: Recent surgery and advanced age are the main concerns; her diabetes and heart failure are unlikely to affect the flight.
Her main concern is glycemic control, while her previous DVT is too remote to be clinically relevant.
Recent surgery, previous DVT, insulin-treated diabetes, stable heart failure, and prolonged travel all need to be considered.
Because her surgery was uncomplicated and her heart failure is stable, no additional assessment is necessary.

questions.text: She will be 9 days post-laparoscopic cholecystectomy on the day of departure. Which statement is most appropriate?
options: Any flight within 2 weeks of abdominal surgery is contraindicated
The timing may be acceptable after uncomplicated laparoscopic surgery if she has recovered well and has no evidence of complications
The flight should be postponed until at least 6 weeks after surgery because of the risk of wound dehiscence
The flight is safe solely because laparoscopic surgery does not affect fitness to fly

questions.text: Before completing the airline's medical form, which of the following is the most appropriate plan for this patient?
options: Continue her usual insulin regimen without modification, encourage oral hydration, and use compression stockings because her previous DVT was 3 years ago.

Develop a time-zone–adjusted insulin and glucose-monitoring plan, assess her need for pharmacological VTE prophylaxis based on her individual risk, and confirm appropriate postoperative recovery and airline arrangements.
Hold her insulin on the day of travel to minimize the risk of hypoglycemia, and use aspirin as VTE prophylaxis because anticoagulation is unnecessary after an uncomplicated laparoscopic procedure.
Delay the flight until she has completed a full 6-week postoperative recovery period, regardless of her clinical status, and restart her usual medications after arrival.
